corrections.was: A Levels window beside a viewport of dots, one dot for each Actor. A level is one playable space, saved as a map file. The Levels window lists the levels in the world, and an eye switches each one on or off. In this made-up example the levels hold twelve, five and forty Actors, fifty-seven in all, and Rooms off leaves seventeen. For example, you could switch off every level but the lighting while you adjust the lights of a large map.
corrections.now: A Levels window beside a viewport of dots, one dot for each Actor. A level is one playable space, saved as a map file. The Levels window lists the levels in the world, and an eye switches each one on or off. For example, you could switch off the Rooms level while you adjust the lights of a large map.
corrections.why: The example switched off every level but Lighting, which would include the Persistent Level, and the slide says the Persistent Level is the one that is always loaded.

corrections.was: A lane with a pickup, a player and a wall, and a table of pairs. Each object has an object type, and a response to every other type, Block, Overlap or Ignore. A pair gets the weaker of its two answers, so Block needs both sides to block. The player and the wall block, and the other two pairs overlap. For example, a spike hazard set to Overlap the player lets the player into it and fires the event that ends the run.
corrections.now: A lane with a pickup, a player and a wall, and a table of pairs. Each object has an object type, and a response to every other type, Block, Overlap or Ignore. A pair gets the weaker of its two answers, so Block needs both sides to block. The player and the wall block, and the other two pairs overlap. For example, a spike hazard set to Overlap the player, with overlap events enabled on both, lets the player into it and fires the event that ends the run.
corrections.why: The example had one side's setting fire the overlap event, but Chapter 4's Unreal section says 'for an overlap to occur, both Actors need to enable Generate Overlap Events' and the slide says Overlap needs both sides to allow overlaps.

corrections.was: A Collision preset is a named bundle of responses, such as BlockAll, OverlapAll or NoCollision, so one choice sets many responses at once. Here the pickup's preset becomes NoCollision. All its responses read Ignore, and the player and pickup pair now reads Ignore too. For example, you would give the outer walls of your level the BlockAll preset, so nothing passes through them, without setting each response by hand.
corrections.now: A Collision preset is a named bundle of responses, such as BlockAll, OverlapAll or NoCollision, so one choice sets many responses at once. Here the pickup's preset becomes NoCollision. All its responses read Ignore, and the player and pickup pair now reads Ignore too. For example, you would give the outer walls of your level the BlockAll preset, so they answer Block to every type, without setting each response by hand.
corrections.why: BlockAll on the walls alone does not stop everything: a pair gets the weaker answer, and the slide's own table shows a Block wall overlapping a pickup, so the claim contradicted the rule just taught.

corrections.was: Make the pickup not block me becomes, set the pickup's response to the player to Overlap, and enable overlap events. The player and pickup pair goes from Block to Overlap, and the player and wall pair stays Block.
corrections.now: Make the pickup not block me becomes, set the pickup's response to the player to Overlap, and enable overlap events on both Actors. The player and pickup pair goes from Block to Overlap, and the player and wall pair stays Block.
corrections.why: Chapter 4's Unreal section says both Actors need Generate Overlap Events; the narration now says so instead of leaving it one-sided.
